cards.headline: Growing fears in Europe regarding the spillover of Russia’s war in Ukraine

Following several reported airspace violations, Polish authorities have stated that further drone and missile strikes are likely. cards.headline: Bangladesh reports 202,000 suspected measles cases during outbreak

pages.text: Bangladesh is managing a measles outbreak that has resulted in 202,000 suspected cases, including 22,000 laboratory-confirmed instances, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). The WHO reported these figures for the period spanning from the start of the outbreak in mid-March through October 9. The number of suspected cases in Bangladesh is higher than any other country this year. The WHO stated that 1,147 people have died from the disease, with 94 percent of those deaths occurring among children under five years old. Experts note that the country's routine vaccination coverage dropped in 2025, falling below the 95 percent threshold the WHO identifies as necessary to prevent outbreaks. Mark Jit, a WHO vaccine adviser and professor at the School of Global Public Health at New York University, described the situation as a real warning to other nations regarding the risks of declining immunization rates. A Reuters review of WHO documents and interviews with health officials and scientists indicated the emergency response was hampered by shortcomings in preparation, inadequate outreach to parents, and data that omitted millions of children.

In September, Ziauddin Hyder, the special assistant on health affairs to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, told Reuters that the government was doing everything possible to end the outbreak. The government did not respond to further questions sent in October.

cards.headline: Israeli settlers attack European diplomats and officials in West Bank

pages.text: Masked Israeli settlers attacked a convoy of European diplomats and officials in the occupied West Bank on Saturday, according to reports from Arab News and The Guardian World. The incident occurred near the village of Taybeh, where a delegation including the French consul general in Jerusalem, the Belgian consul, and the Polish consul were participating in an olive harvest on lands belonging to the Christian town. Witnesses reported that a group of seven men, some armed with clubs, arrived on all-terrain vehicles, surrounded the convoy, and demanded identification documents. During the confrontation, a window of an armored car belonging to the Belgian mission was smashed, and three people were injured. Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of the French town Aulnoye-Aymeries, was reportedly assaulted and knocked to the ground while attempting to enter a vehicle with diplomatic plates. The group also allegedly threatened Baudoux’s wife and Vincent Dollmann, the archbishop of Cambrai. One witness stated a masked militant shouted “Vive la France” during the attack. Belgian Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Maxime Prévot condemned the violence, stating that the country would continue to push for European Union sanctions on settlers. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot demanded that Israeli authorities arrest those responsible and halt the violence. The Israeli military condemned the attack as a severe act of violence and stated that police had opened an investigation, noting that the delegation’s tour had not been coordinated with Israeli forces and no soldiers were present at the scene. Meanwhile, the office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu suggested the reports might be part of a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and its residents during the annual olive harvest.

The assault on diplomats followed a separate incident on Friday in which Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine was injured by Israeli settlers near the village of Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah. Levine, who was wearing a press vest and helmet, reported being pushed to the ground and kicked by a group of settlers while photographing Palestinian farmers harvesting olives. According to The Guardian World and NPR World, the attack lasted more than 10 minutes and resulted in the theft of her passport, phone, wallet, and equipment. Levine was treated at a hospital in Ramallah. The Washington Post denounced the attack and called for a thorough investigation. Palestinian authorities reported that attacks in eight villages resulted in injuries to at least 20 people. cards.headline: TIB alleges state reforms in Bangladesh are being hindered by power politics and bureaucracy

pages.text: Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) stated in a statement on October 17, 2026, that the potential for establishing an accountable government system and reforming the state following the July mass uprising is being hindered by bureaucratic influence and power politics. TIB Executive Director Iftekharuzzaman noted that while there was a commitment in the 31-point demand and election manifesto to implement state reforms and the July National Charter, uncertainty has arisen because members of parliament from the winning party did not take the oath as members of the proposed Constitutional Reform Commission. Iftekharuzzaman stated that the process of institutional reform, lawmaking, and constitutional amendment is now dependent on the inclinations of the ruling coalition. He further noted that of the 133 ordinances issued by the interim government, only those strengthening the executive branch have been passed into law, while ordinances intended to establish accountability have been suspended or repealed. TIB also reported that the opposition coalition is focused on partisan political interests rather than supporting state reform for the public interest.

The TIB statement raised several specific concerns regarding judicial and institutional independence. The organization questioned the government's role in ensuring judicial independence, noting that the repeal of the Supreme Court Judges Appointment Ordinance and the Supreme Court Secretariat (Amendment) Ordinance represents a stance opposed to state reform. Regarding the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC), TIB stated that failing to convert the ACC Amendment Ordinance into law and instead reverting to the 2004 law has obstructed efforts to overcome the commission's trust deficit. TIB also expressed concern over the National Human Rights Commission, stating that repealing its related ordinance to enact a new law conflicts with international standards and public aspirations for an independent commission. Additionally, the organization noted that the repeal of the Disappearances Prevention and Remedy Ordinance may protect agencies responsible for human rights violations. TIB criticized the decision to provide the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) with a new identity to make it more powerful instead of dissolving it, and noted that no initiatives have been taken to form an independent police commission despite political consensus. Finally, Iftekharuzzaman observed that despite a consensus on elected representatives publishing asset details within three months of assuming office, no such practices have been reflected since members of parliament were sworn in.

cards.headline: HRW alleges Syrian authorities are restricting women's admission to defense and security university programs

pages.text: Human Rights Watch (HRW) stated on October 16, 2026, that Syrian authorities are discriminating against women by restricting their admission to most programs at two newly established state universities specializing in defense and security. The rights group urged the government to lift these restrictions before applications close on October 19. According to HRW, the Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research announced on September 30 that admission to law, economics and management, and social sciences programs at the National University of Defense Sciences is reserved for men. At the Syrian University for Security Sciences, women are reportedly only permitted to apply to cybersecurity programs. Hiba Zayadin, a senior Syria advisor for HRW, said the restrictions prevent women from training as military officers or pursuing careers as administrators and lawyers within the army. Zayadin stated that authorities are rebuilding the security forces and army without women.

At the National University of Defense Sciences, men-only admission rules apply to the College of Humanities and Administrative Sciences, as well as the land, naval, and air force military colleges. The university’s Higher Institute for Applied Sciences and Technology is the only section open to women, though it does not require graduates to serve in the military. At the Syrian University for Security Sciences, the Technical Institute of Security Sciences and the College of Security Sciences also admit men only. HRW called on the Ministry of Higher Education to repeal gender-based admissions restrictions and open the programs to women on equal terms. The organization indicated that these policies contradict commitments made by transitional authorities to uphold women's rights and equality, and may undermine women's participation in Syria's political transition.

Lieberman described the international wildlife trade for species such as reptiles and amphibians as a massive experiment regarding the movement of diseases between different parts of the world. Altherr stated that the exotic pet trade could be regulated very quickly to reduce these risks. The experts identified several legal gaps that governments could address, including the lack of legal recourse for countries of origin when species are sold outside their borders. The Palestinian Education Ministry also reported significant damage to educational facilities. In Gaza, the ministry states that more than 179 government schools have been completely destroyed and 105 UNRWA schools have been damaged.

cards.headline: Syria states it has no plans to open new fronts in Yemen war

pages.text: Syria stated on Wednesday that it has no plans to open new fronts in the conflict in Yemen, despite reports suggesting the country was considering military assistance to Saudi Arabia. The Syrian Ministry of Information’s Foreign Media Department said the nation stands with Saudi Arabia against threats to its security and stability, but emphasized that its regional policy is based on peace, stability, and cooperation. This statement follows a Reuters report citing U.S. and Syrian officials who said Damascus was considering providing military assistance to Riyadh amid the escalating conflict with the Iran-backed Houthi movement. The ministry described its absolute priority as rebuilding the country, strengthening state institutions, and working with partners on reconstruction and improving living conditions for Syrians. It added that any military cooperation with partner countries would occur only through official channels and within existing bilateral frameworks.

cards.headline: ASEAN energy ministers meet in Manila to discuss fuel security amid Middle East conflict

pages.text: Energy ministers from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) gathered in Manila on Wednesday for talks regarding energy security. According to Arab News, the meeting aims to reduce the region's dependence on supply chains affected by the conflict between the United States, Israel, and Iran. Since February, US-Israeli attacks on Iran and retaliatory strikes by Tehran on American allies in the Gulf region have disrupted maritime access, shipping security, and energy transport costs through the Strait of Hormuz. Attacks on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz have intensified since September, while Houthi strikes targeting Saudi Arabia have increased pressure on the Bab Al-Mandab Strait waterway. The meeting occurs as oil prices have risen above $100 a barrel. ASEAN Secretary-General Dr. Kao Kim Hourn addressed the ministers, stating that geopolitical developments and supply disruptions affect energy markets, supply chains, and the reliability of energy supplies. A policy paper released last week by the ASEAN Centre for Energy warned that severe disruptions to Middle East supplies could put nearly 28 percent of the bloc's final oil consumption at risk. The region, which has a population of 700 million, imports over 55 percent of the crude for its refineries from the Middle East. Dependence on Middle East power imports varies among member states, ranging from approximately one-quarter of crude in some markets to more than four-fifths in others. Data from the ASEAN Centre for Energy indicates that petrol retail prices have increased by 76 percent in the Philippines and 68 percent in Cambodia, while diesel prices in Thailand surged by 70 percent. Additionally, supply shortages have triggered emergency contract suspensions at petrochemical companies in Singapore and Indonesia due to the movement of over a third of global urea exports through the Gulf.

cards.headline: Annual job creation in Bangladesh lags behind labor market entry, World Bank report finds

pages.text: Between 2016 and 2024, approximately 2 million people entered the labor market in Bangladesh each year, while only about 900,000 new jobs were created annually, according to a special chapter in the World Bank's 2026 Bangladesh Development update report. The report, titled “What Business Environment is Needed to Boost Employment,” notes that seven out of every 10 new jobs were in agriculture, while employment in the industrial sector decreased. For women, the report states that while 4.2 million new jobs were created in agriculture, industrial jobs decreased by 1.1 million and service sector jobs decreased by 800,000. Consequently, female labor force participation dropped from 42.8% in 2022 to 38.4% in 2024.

The World Bank assessment describes a “productivity paradox” in Bangladesh, noting that while the economy grew at an average annual rate of 6% from fiscal year 2015-16 to 2024-25, progress in productivity, investment, and new business creation at the firm level has not kept pace. The report indicates that the top 10% of firms by productivity control 75% of total sales in the formal sector but account for only 15% of employment. Other businesses face obstacles including complex government procedures, lack of financing, unfair competition, and power shortages. Senior managers spend an average of 13% of their time dealing with government regulations, and 71% of firms experience power outages, which costs them approximately 9% of their annual sales. The report draws on data from the World Bank Enterprise Survey 2022, Business Ready 2025, Business of the State 2019, Bangladesh Country Private Sector Diagnostic 2025, and UNCTAD investment data.

cards.headline: Former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega intends to run for FIFA president

pages.text: Ramon Vega, a 55-year-old former Switzerland centre-back who played for Tottenham Hotspur, Celtic, and Watford, has announced his intention to stand as a candidate in next year's FIFA presidential election. Vega is the first person to confirm a challenge to current president Gianni Infantino. In a statement, Vega said he is standing to reunite the global football family, deliver reform, modernize FIFA, and rebuild trust in the game. He added that his life has prepared him to serve the sport, which he described as belonging to players, coaches, supporters, and communities rather than administrators. Since retiring from football in 2004, Vega has worked in finance. He previously considered running for the position in 2015 following the suspension of former president Sepp Blatter, and expressed intent to stand against Infantino four years later, though he did not secure the backing of five of FIFA's 211 member federations required to be included in the ballot. To qualify, candidates must be proposed by a member association, have played an active role in the game for two of the past five years, and pass an eligibility check by a review committee.

cards.headline: Study finds scientists with high faith in technology less likely to take climate action

pages.text: A study from the London School of Economics, published in Environmental Research Letters, found that scientists who believe technology will largely solve the problems caused by the climate crisis are less likely to engage in civic action or lifestyle changes. The research surveyed more than 9,000 scientists across 115 countries regarding their views on “techno-optimism.” Of those surveyed, 27% agreed that technology will largely solve climate change problems, while 44% disagreed and 29% neither agreed nor disagreed. The report found that techno-optimism was most prevalent among scientists working in applied and natural sciences and those with right-leaning political views. Lead author Fabian Dablander stated that the belief in technological solutions can lead to an over-reliance on unproven solutions at the expense of necessary socioeconomic transformations, noting that technological solutions are often politically attractive because they do not require changes to how people live and consume.

According to the London School of Economics report, “techno-optimist” scientists are 23% less likely to sign petitions or participate in protests than peers who doubt technology is the answer. These scientists also reported engaging in less advocacy and fewer civic actions. Additionally, the study found that techno-optimists are 18% less likely to make high-impact lifestyle changes, such as reducing flights, cutting car usage, or adopting a mostly vegan or vegetarian diet. Dablander noted that while technology cannot substitute for broader societal changes and large-scale shifts in consumption, there is a tendency at the individual level for greater faith in technological solutions to go hand in hand with less engagement in climate action.
